---
id: 'auth-third-party-custom-oidc'
title: 'Custom OIDC provider'
subtitle: 'Use any OIDC-compliant identity provider with your Supabase project'
---

Any identity provider that supports OpenID Connect (OIDC) can be used as a third-party authentication provider alongside Supabase Auth, or standalone, with your Supabase project. Use this guide for a provider that is not in the list of [supported providers](/docs/guides/auth/third-party/overview).

## Getting started

1. Check that your provider meets the [requirements](#requirements).
2. Add a Third-Party Auth integration with your provider's issuer URL in the [Dashboard](#add-the-integration-in-the-dashboard) or with the [Management API](#add-the-integration-with-the-management-api).
3. Add the `role` claim to the JWTs your provider issues.
4. Set up the Supabase client in your application.

## Requirements

Your provider must meet the [limitations](/docs/guides/auth/third-party/overview#limitations) of third-party auth:

1. It exposes an OIDC Issuer Discovery URL, served at `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`.
2. It signs JWTs with an asymmetric key and includes a `kid` header parameter. Symmetrically signed JWTs, such as HS256, are not supported.
3. Its JWTs contain a `role` claim. See [Assign the role claim](#assign-the-role-claim).

The issuer URL must use HTTPS. Your project reads the signing keys from the `jwks_uri` listed in the discovery document.

## Add the integration in the Dashboard

1. In the Dashboard, go to **Authentication** > **Sign In / Providers** > [**Third-Party Auth**](/dashboard/project/_/auth/third-party).
2. Click **Add provider** and select **Custom OIDC**.
3. Enter your provider's issuer URL in **Issuer URL**, for example `https://login.example.com`.
4. Click **Add provider**.

The provider appears in the Third-Party Auth list with its issuer URL. To remove it, delete it from the same list.

## Add the integration with the Management API

Create a [personal access token](/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens), then call the [create third-party auth integration](/docs/reference/api/v1-create-project-tpa-integration) endpoint with your issuer URL:

```bash
export PROJECT_REF="your-project-ref"

curl -X POST "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/config/auth/third-party-auth" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "oidc_issuer_url": "https://login.example.com"
  }'
```

The response includes the integration `id`. To list or remove integrations, use the [list](/docs/reference/api/v1-list-project-tpa-integrations) and [delete](/docs/reference/api/v1-delete-project-tpa-integration) endpoints.

<Admonition type="note">

The Supabase CLI has no `supabase/config.toml` key for custom OIDC providers. Add the integration in the Dashboard or with the Management API.

</Admonition>

## Assign the role claim

Your Supabase project inspects the `role` claim in every JWT sent to it, to assign the correct Postgres role when using the Data API, Storage or Realtime authorization. Without a `role` claim, requests run as the `anon` role.

Set `role` to `authenticated` for signed-in users. Use your provider's custom claims or token template feature to add it. See your provider's documentation for the steps.

## Set up the Supabase client library

Pass an `accessToken` async function that returns your provider's JWT for the current user, or `null` if there is no signed-in user:

```typescript
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

const supabase = createClient(
  'https://<supabase-project>.supabase.co',
  'SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
  {
    accessToken: async () => {
      return getAccessTokenFromYourProvider()
    },
  }
)
```

Replace `getAccessTokenFromYourProvider` with the call your provider's SDK offers to get the current user's JWT.

## Using RLS policies

After the client sends your provider's JWT, use RLS policies to secure access to your project's database, Storage objects and Realtime channels.

### Identify the user

The `sub` claim identifies the user. `auth.uid()` casts `sub` to `uuid`, so it fails if your provider issues subjects that are not UUIDs. Read the claim directly instead:

```sql
create policy "Users can read their own rows"
  on table_name
  for select
  to authenticated
  using (user_id = (select auth.jwt()->>'sub'));
```

Here `user_id` must be a `text` column.

### Restrict access by issuer

Your project trusts every issuer you add, and `sub` values from different issuers can collide. If you use more than one issuer, or you also use Supabase Auth, add a restrictive policy that checks the `iss` claim:

```sql
create policy "Restrict access to trusted issuers"
  on table_name
  as restrictive
  to authenticated
  using (
    (auth.jwt()->>'iss' = 'https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1')
    or
    (auth.jwt()->>'iss' = 'https://login.example.com')
  );
```

<Admonition type="danger">

Postgres has two types of policies: permissive and restrictive. This example uses a restrictive policy, so make sure you don't omit the `as restrictive` clause.

</Admonition>

For more on restrictive policies and on sharing the check across tables, Storage and Realtime, see the [Firebase Auth guide](/docs/guides/auth/third-party/firebase-auth#adding-an-extra-layer-of-security-to-your-projects-rls-policies-self-hosting-only).
